dedupe_keys.name: north america space weather impact on the power grid from insurance claims for electrical equipment 2000 to 2010

description: This case study measures how space weather affects electrical equipment in North America through a statistical analysis of 11,242 commercial insurance claims from 2000 to 2010 for losses and business interruptions linked to damaged or malfunctioning electrical and electronic equipment. Carolus Schrijver, Robert Dobbins, William Murtagh and Stephen Petrinec posted it in June 2014 to test whether geomagnetically induced currents reach the low-voltage distribution network. Claims rates are about 20 percent higher on the top 5 percent of days by geomagnetic variability and about 10 percent higher on the most active third; surge-related claims follow the same dependence as major disturbances of the U.S. high-voltage grid, suggesting about 500 claims in an average year. Coverage is continental North America at daily resolution. Format and access: an open preprint with PDF on arXiv. Licence: arXiv distribution licence; free to read. Caveats: the claims data are an insurer's portfolio and are not released, and attribution is statistical, not per event. It serves hazard exposure and resilience analysis of space weather for grids and customer equipment. Related catalogue records are the NOAA NCEI satellite anomalies archive and the Hydro-Québec 1989 blackout.
